'''''Vicia sativa''''', known as the '''common vetch''', '''garden vetch''', '''tare''' or simply '''vetch''', is a [[Nitrogen fixation|nitrogen-fixing]] [[legume|leguminous]] plant in the family [[Fabaceae]]. It is now naturalised throughout the world, being absent only  in [[Antarctica]] and the [[Arctic]] regions.<ref>Ian C. Murfet and Kristin L. Groom. "Vicia Sativa Aggregate." ''Handbook of Flowering, Volume VI.'' Abraham Halevy, ed. CRC Press, 2019. [https://books.google.com/books?id=MySlDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT1078 Page .] {{ISBN|9781351089487}}</ref> The centre of diversity is thought to be the [[Fertile Crescent]], although gold standard molecular confirmation is currently not available. 

Global common vetch cultivation is limited due to anti-nutritional compounds in the seed although it is grown in dryland agricultural zones in Australia, China and Ethiopia due to its drought tolerance and very low nutrient requirements compared to other legumes. In these agricultural zones common vetch is grown as a [[green manure]], [[livestock]] [[fodder]] or [[Crop rotation|rotation crop.]] In cultivated grainfields, like [[Lentil|lentils]], it is often considered a [[weed]] due to downgrading of harvested mixed grain, resulting in farmers receiving less financial returns.

==Description==
''Vicia sativa'' is a sprawling [[annual herb]], with hollow, four-sided, hairless to sparsely hairy stems which can reach two meters in maximum length.

The leaves are [[stipule|stipulate]], alternate and compound, each made up of 3–8 opposite pairs of linear, lance-shaped, oblong, or wedge-shaped, needle-tipped [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]] up to {{convert|35|mm|frac=4|sp=us}} long. Each [[compound leaf]] ends in a branched [[tendril]].

The pea-like flowers occur in the leaf axils, solitary or in pairs. The [[flower corolla]] is {{convert|1|-|3|cm|frac=4|sp=us}} long and bright pink-purple in colour, more rarely whitish or yellow. The flowers are mostly visited by [[bumblebee]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers |name-list-style=amp |journal = [[Plant Biology (journal)|Plant Biology]] | pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = van der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762 | pmid=25754608 | volume=18| issue = 1| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

The fruit is a [[legume]] pod up to {{convert|6|or|7|cm|frac=4|sp=us}} long, which is hairy when new, smooth later, then brown or black when ripe. It contains 4–12 seeds.<ref name="Blamey-2003">{{cite book |last1=Blamey |first1=M. |last2=Fitter |first2=R. |last3=Fitter |first3=A. |name-list-style=amp |year=2003 |title=Wild flowers of Britain and Ireland: The Complete Guide to the British and Irish Flora |publisher=A & C Black |location=London |isbn=978-1-4081-7950-5 |page=142}}</ref><ref name="Stace-2010">{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. ==Cultivation==
{{How-to|section|date=December 2022}}
[[File:Vesce poëlée.jpg|thumb|200px|Cooked vetch (''Vicia sativa'')]]
Sown for [[fodder]],<ref>{{cite book |editor=Hackney, P. |year=1992 |title=Stewart and Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland |edition=3rd |publisher=Queen's University Belfast |isbn=0-85389-446-9}}</ref> the [[seed]] is [[sowing|sown]] densely, up to {{convert|250|kg/ha}}. However, when grown for seed, less seed is used so that the crop is not too thick, which reduces flower and seed production. When meant for seed, sowing is done early in the planting season for good returns; but, when for green manure, any time in spring is suitable. Sometimes, a full crop can be obtained even when sown as late as summer, though sowing so late is not recommended.<ref name="Kelly-1881">{{cite book |title=The Household Cyclopedia of General Information |publisher=Thomas Kelly |location=New York |year=1881 |page=47 |url=https://archive.org/stream/Household_Cyclopedia#page/n45/mode/2up}}</ref>

After the seed is sown and the land carefully [[harrow (tool)|harrowed]], a light [[roller (agricultural tool)|roller]] ought to be drawn across, to smooth the surface and permit the [[scythe]] to work without interruption. Also, the field should be watched for several days to prevent [[pigeon]]s from eating too much of the sown seed.<ref name="Kelly-1881"/>

[[Horse]]s thrive very well on common vetch, even better than on [[clover]] and [[rye grass]]; the same applies to fattening [[cattle]], which feed faster on vetch than on most [[Poaceae|grasses]] or other edible plants. Danger often arises from livestock eating too much vetch, especially when podded; [[colic]]s and other [[stomach]] disorders are apt to be produced by the excessive amounts devoured.<ref name="Kelly-1881"/>

[[Cereal]] grains can be sown with vetch so it can use their stronger stems for support, attaching via [[tendril]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/AG/aGA/AGAP/FRG/AFRIS/Data/297.HTM |title=FAO Animal Feed Resources |access-date=2010-11-22 |archive-date=2012-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024200353/http://www.fao.org/AG/aGA/AGAP/FRG/AFRIS/Data/297.HTM  }}</ref> When grown with [[oat]]s or other [[grass]]es, the vetch can grow upright; otherwise its weak stems may sprawl along the ground.<ref name="FAO Crop Profile">{{Cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/AG/agp/agpc/doc/Gbase/DATA/Pf000505.HTM |title=FAO Crop Profile |access-date=2010-11-22 |archive-date=2017-11-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171115123829/http://www.fao.org/ag/agp/agpc/doc/gbase/data/pf000505.htm  }}</ref> Several [[cultivar]]s are available for agricultural use,<ref>{{cite book |author=Lloveras, J. |author2=Santiveri, P. |author3=Vendrell, A. |author4=Torrent, D. |author5=Ballesta, A. |chapter-url=http://ressources.ciheam.org/om/pdf/c62/04600139.pdf |chapter=Varieties of vetch (''Vicia sativa'' L.) for forage and grain production in Mediterranean areas |editor1=A. Ferchichi |title=Réhabilitation des pâturages et des parcours en milieux méditerranéens |location=Zaragoza |publisher=CIHEAM |year=2004 |pages=103–106 |series=Cahiers Options Méditerranéennes |volume=62 |access-date=2010-11-22 |archive-date=2017-03-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170324175138/http://ressources.ciheam.org/om/pdf/c62/04600139.pdf  }}</ref> and as for some other legume crops, [[rhizobia]] can be added to the seed.<ref name="FAO Crop Profile"/>

Pests that attack this crop include the [[powdery mildew]] fungus ''[[Erysiphe baeumleri]]'', the pea aphid ''[[Acyrthosiphon pisum]]'', the [[Helicoverpa zea|corn earworm]] (''Heliothis zea''), the [[fall armyworm]] (''Spodoptera frugiperda''), and [[spider mite]]s of genus ''[[Tetranychus]]''.<ref name="FAO Crop Profile"/>

During the early 20th century, a mutant of the common vetch arose with lens-shaped seeds resembling those of the [[lentil]], leading to vetch invasions of lentil fields. [[D. G. Rowlands]] showed in 1959 that this was due to a single [[recessive]] mutation. The transition from traditional [[winnowing]] to [[mechanised agriculture|mechanised farming]] practices largely solved this problem.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Fred Gould |year=1991 |title=The evolutionary potential of crop pests |journal=[[American Scientist]] |volume=79 |issue=6 |pages=496–507 |bibcode=1991AmSci..79..496G |url=http://www4.ncsu.edu/~fgould/pdfs/Gould1991.pdf |archive-date=2016-02-07 |access-date=2012-03-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160207153300/http://www4.ncsu.edu/~fgould/pdfs/Gould1991.pdf }}</ref>

Improved varieties of ''Vicia sativa'' developed by the National Vetch Breeding Program for [[Australia|Australian farmers]] include; Timok, Volga, Rasina and more recently Studenica. These varieties are mostly cultivated in Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria. More than {{convert|500000|ha}} per year of ''Vicia sativa'' was grown in [[Australia]] in 2019.

==History==
Common vetch has long been part of the human diet, as attested by carbonised remains found at early [[Neolithic]] sites in Syria, Turkey, Bulgaria, Hungary and Slovakia. It has also been reported from [[Predynastic]] sites of [[ancient Egypt]], and several Bronze Age sites in [[Turkmenistan|Turkmenia]] and Slovakia. However, definite evidence for later vetch cultivation is available only for [[ancient Rome|Roman]] times.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Daniel Zohary |author2=Maria Hopf |year=2000 |title=Domestication of Plants in the Old World |edition=3rd |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-850356-9 |page=119}}</ref>

Although ''V. sativa'' is sometimes known as tare, the "tare" referred to in some English translations of the [[Bible]] (as in the "[[Parable of the Tares]]") is thought to be darnel ryegrass, ''[[Lolium temulentum]]''.<ref name="Cope-2009">{{cite book|first1=T.|last1=Cope|first2=A.|last2=Gray|date=2009|title=Grasses of the British Isles. BSBI Handbook No. 13 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=London |isbn=978-0-901158-42-0 }}</ref>{{rp|162}}

== Genome ==
The ''Vicia sativa'' [[karyotype]] consists of 5, 6 or 7 [[chromosome]]s, with six (n=6) being the most common and best described.<ref name="Navratilova-2003">{{Cite journal|last1=NAVRÁTILOVÁ|first1=ALICE|last2=NEUMANN|first2=PAVEL|last3=MACAS|first3=JIŘÍ|date=June 2003|title=Karyotype Analysis of Four Vicia Species using In Situ Hybridization with Repetitive Sequences|journal=Annals of Botany|volume=91|issue=7|pages=921–926|doi=10.1093/aob/mcg099|issn=0305-7364|pmc=4242401|pmid=12770847}}</ref> Given the ''Vicia sativa's'' genome is relatively large genome size (1.75[[Gigabase|Gb]]) due to large amounts of repetitive DNA,<ref name="Navratilova-2003"/> sequencing the genome was challenging compared to other legumes such as ''[[Medicago truncatula]]'' or [[soybean]]s.

A high-quality chromosome level genome assembly was published in 2022<ref name="Xi-2022">{{cite journal |biorxiv=10.1101/2021.10.11.464017|doi=10.46471/gigabyte.38 |title=Chromosome-level assembly of the common vetch (Vicia sativa) reference genome |date=2022 |last1=Xi |first1=Hangwei |last2=Nguyen |first2=Vy |last3=Ward |first3=Christopher |last4=Liu |first4=Zhipeng |last5=Searle |first5=Iain R. |journal=Gigabyte |pages=1–20 |pmid=36824524 |pmc=9650280 }}</ref> of variety Studencia (n=6), following a draft genome assembly of line KSR5 (n=7). Variety Studencia, is predicted to have 53,318 protein coding genes.<ref name="Xi-2022"/> Whole genome sequence comparisons showed that ''Vicia sativa'' is most closely related to [[pea]].<ref name="Xi-2022" />

A high-quality genome sequence facilitates the application of [[genome editing]] and genomic selection for healthy, higher yielding varieties.
